Many peptides are not approved for human use and are sold by others only as research compounds, so a licensed healthcare provider should always be consulted before acting on anything here. home.heroTitle: Turn any dose into the exact amount to draw.
home.heroBody: A free calculator for people new to peptides. Entering the vial contents and the dose returns the exact amount to draw on the syringe, in mcg, mg, or units. No sign-up. Just the math.
home.problemTitle: mg, mcg, units. Where it gets confusing.
home.problemBody: A vial, some bacteriostatic water, a syringe, and a pile of numbers that don’t obviously fit together. mg? mcg? units? The internet is full of bro-science, sketchy vendors, and people trying to sell something. BuddyPept explains the math, clearly.
home.whatBody: BuddyPept is a free calculator and plain-English guide for people new to peptides. Entering the vial contents and a dose returns the exact equivalent amount, in whatever unit the syringe uses. That is the whole thing.
home.howStep1: Pick a peptide, or request one that is not listed yet.
home.howStep2: Enter the vial amount, the bacteriostatic water, and a dose.
home.howStep3: See it in mcg, mg, and syringe units, clearly explained.

warning.doseBelowOneUnit: Dose is less than 1 syringe unit, so measurement accuracy is poor at this scale. Consider reconstituting with less bacteriostatic water for a higher concentration.

warning.concentrationVeryHigh: Very high peptide concentration. Double-check the vial fully dissolved and that the bacteriostatic water amount is correct.
warning.iuNotConvertible: IU (International Units) cannot be reliably converted to mass without substance-specific bioactivity data. Consult the peptide manufacturer or a healthcare professional for the correct IU-to-mass conversion for the specific compound.
warning.exceedsBarrel: This dose needs {ml} mL, more than the {syringe} holds ({max} mL). Use a larger syringe, or mix with more water for a weaker concentration.

disclaimer.title: Medical Disclaimer
intro: BuddyPept is a free educational tool that helps people understand peptide reconstitution and dosing math. Read this page before using the calculator or anything else on the site.

sections.title: This is education, not medical advice
sections.body: Everything on BuddyPept is for general informational and educational purposes only. It is not medical advice, and it is not a substitute for the judgment of a licensed healthcare provider. BuddyPept does not diagnose conditions, treat illness, prescribe anything, or state whether a peptide is safe or appropriate for any person.

sections.title: BuddyPept does not recommend doses
sections.body: The calculator performs only the math requested. The user enters the amounts (the vial contents, the amount of water, the intended dose), and the calculator converts those numbers between units. It never suggests a dose, a frequency, or a protocol. Any dose entered is one decided by the user together with a healthcare provider, not one chosen by BuddyPept.

sections.title: No doctor-patient relationship
sections.body: Use of this website does not create a doctor-patient, provider-patient, or any professional relationship between the user and BuddyPept or anyone associated with it. BuddyPept is not a healthcare provider.

sections.title: Not evaluated by the FDA
sections.body: The statements on this website have not been evaluated by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration. Nothing on BuddyPept is intended to diagnose, treat, cure, or prevent any disease.

sections.title: About peptides specifically
sections.body: Many peptides are not approved by the FDA or other regulators for human use, and their legal status varies by country and over time. Companies that sell them often do so strictly as research compounds, labeled “for research use only” and “not for human consumption.” BuddyPept explains the math and the science. It does not sell these compounds, does not encourage anyone to use them in a person, and does not state that doing so is safe or legal. Whether a peptide is legal in a given location, and whether any use is appropriate, is for the user and a licensed professional to decide. The user is responsible for following the laws that apply to them.

sections.title: Accuracy and user responsibility
sections.body: BuddyPept works to keep the math correct, but cannot guarantee that any result is accurate or appropriate for a specific situation. Always verify any result against the vial label and a licensed provider’s guidance before acting on it. The user is responsible for verifying the numbers entered and the numbers acted on.

privacy.title: Privacy Policy
intro: Privacy is part of how BuddyPept is built. Collection is kept to the bare minimum, and data is never sold.

sections.title: What is collected
body: The calculator is free, requires no sign-up, and collects nothing. A name and email address are collected only when the “request a peptide” form is submitted, along with the name of the peptide requested.
Other research tools may request investigator information when needed. Any such information is provided voluntarily and collected only with the investigator’s knowledge and consent.
BuddyPept continues to add tools, so what is collected may change over time. This policy is updated whenever it does.

sections.title: What is not collected
body: The BuddyPept calculator does not request or store personal health information. Calculator inputs are processed in the browser only to generate results and are not saved.
BuddyPept does not use third-party advertising or tracking pixels.

sections.title: How the information is used
sections.body: The name and email are used for one purpose: to give notice by email when the requested peptide is added to the library. Addresses are not added to unrelated marketing without consent.

sections.title: Who it is shared with
sections.body: Personal information is never sold. A small number of trusted service providers run the site, covering hosting, database, and email delivery. They process data only to provide those services to BuddyPept. Information is shared with them only as needed for that purpose, or if required by law.

sections.title: Retention and choices
sections.body: A request is kept only as long as needed to follow up on it. A request to see the stored information, or to delete it, can be made at any time by email, and it will be honored.

sections.title: Security
sections.body: Reasonable steps are taken to protect personal information, but no method of storage or transmission over the internet is completely secure, so absolute security cannot be guaranteed.

sections.title: Children
sections.body: BuddyPept is not directed to children and is intended for adults. Information from minors is not knowingly collected.

sections.title: Changes
sections.body: If this policy changes, the date at the top of this page is updated.

semaglutide.teaser: An FDA-approved GLP-1 medicine for diabetes and weight.
semaglutide.studiedFor: FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes (Ozempic) and weight management (Wegovy), and studied in large clinical trials. Rybelsus is an oral form for diabetes.
semaglutide.howSold: By prescription as a pre-filled pen or vial (Ozempic, Wegovy) or tablets (Rybelsus). It is also sold by gray-market vendors as a research powder, which is not the approved product.
semaglutide.bottomLine: Semaglutide is an FDA-approved prescription medicine. The approved product comes through a licensed provider and pharmacy, and decisions about it belong with them.

bpc-157.teaser: A lab-made peptide studied in animals for tissue repair.
bpc-157.whatItIs: A synthetic peptide, a short chain of amino acids based on a sequence found in a protein in gastric juice. It is made in a lab.
bpc-157.studiedFor: In published preclinical work, mostly animal and laboratory studies, it has been examined for tissue repair, tendon and ligament healing, and gastrointestinal effects. These are early research findings, not proven results in people.
bpc-157.howSold: As a freeze-dried powder in glass vials, commonly 5 mg or 10 mg, mixed with bacteriostatic water before use.
bpc-157.bottomLine: The science is early and mostly preclinical. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

tb-500.teaser: A synthetic fragment of a natural protein, studied for repair.
tb-500.whatItIs: A synthetic version of a fragment of thymosin beta-4, a protein that occurs naturally in the body. It is made in a lab.
tb-500.studiedFor: Preclinical studies have looked at it for tissue repair, wound healing, and inflammation in animal and laboratory models. These are research findings, not proven effects in people.
tb-500.howSold: As a freeze-dried powder in glass vials, commonly 5 mg or 10 mg, reconstituted with bacteriostatic water.
tb-500.bottomLine: The evidence is largely preclinical. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

ghk-cu.teaser: A copper peptide common in skincare and studied for repair.
ghk-cu.whatItIs: A copper-binding peptide (copper tripeptide-1) that occurs naturally in human plasma, with levels that decline with age. It is produced synthetically for products.
ghk-cu.studiedFor: Studied for skin remodeling, hair, and wound healing. It is widely used in topical cosmetics and has been examined as an injectable in research settings.
ghk-cu.howSold: As a powder in vials (often 50 mg or 100 mg) for reconstitution, and in many topical skincare products.
ghk-cu.bottomLine: Topical cosmetic use is common; injectable use is research-stage. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

ipamorelin.teaser: A peptide studied for how the body releases growth hormone.
ipamorelin.whatItIs: A synthetic peptide that signals the pituitary gland. It is classed as a growth hormone secretagogue.
ipamorelin.studiedFor: Researched for its effect on the body’s own growth hormone release, often discussed alongside CJC-1295. Findings are largely preclinical.
ipamorelin.howSold: As a powder in vials (commonly 2, 5, or 10 mg), reconstituted with bacteriostatic water. Often paired with CJC-1295.
ipamorelin.bottomLine: The research is early. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

cjc-1295-dac.teaser: A long-acting GHRH analog dosed weekly rather than daily.
cjc-1295-dac.whatItIs: A synthetic analog of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH) carrying a Drug Affinity Complex, or DAC. The DAC binds to serum albumin in the blood, which is what keeps the molecule circulating for days instead of minutes.
cjc-1295-dac.studiedFor: Examined for its influence on the body’s own growth hormone release. Published work reports a half-life of roughly 6 to 8 days, which is the property the DAC exists to create. Findings are largely preclinical.
cjc-1295-dac.howSold: As a powder in vials, commonly 2 or 5 mg, reconstituted with bacteriostatic water. Sold by research suppliers, not as an approved medicine.
cjc-1295-dac.bottomLine: The DAC is the whole difference. It is dosed on a weekly rhythm because it clears over days, and it is not interchangeable with the no-DAC version. The research is early. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

cjc-1295-no-dac.teaser: Modified GRF (1-29), a short-acting GHRH analog.
cjc-1295-no-dac.whatItIs: A synthetic analog of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH) without the Drug Affinity Complex. The molecule is more precisely called Modified GRF (1-29), and it carries no albumin-binding group.
cjc-1295-no-dac.studiedFor: Examined for its influence on the body’s own growth hormone release, and commonly studied together with ipamorelin. Published work reports a half-life of roughly 30 minutes. Findings are largely preclinical.
cjc-1295-no-dac.howSold: As a powder in vials, commonly 2, 5 or 10 mg, reconstituted with bacteriostatic water. Sold by research suppliers, not as an approved medicine.
cjc-1295-no-dac.bottomLine: Despite sharing a name, this is not the DAC version on a different schedule. It clears in about half an hour rather than over days, which is why it appears in protocols at a very different frequency. The research is early. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

sermorelin.teaser: A prescription GHRH analog used in some hormone protocols.
sermorelin.whatItIs: A synthetic analog of growth hormone releasing hormone (GHRH).
sermorelin.studiedFor: FDA-approved (as Geref) for diagnostic testing of pituitary function, and prescribed off-label in some anti-aging and hormone protocols.
sermorelin.howSold: By prescription, including from compounding pharmacies, as a powder for reconstitution (commonly 2 to 15 mg vials).
sermorelin.bottomLine: Sermorelin is a prescription medication. Whether it is appropriate for a given person is a decision for them and a licensed healthcare provider.

retatrutide.teaser: An investigational metabolic peptide, still in clinical trials.
retatrutide.whatItIs: An investigational peptide that acts on three receptors (GLP-1, GIP, and glucagon).
retatrutide.studiedFor: Being tested in clinical trials for metabolic conditions such as obesity and type 2 diabetes. It is not yet approved for any use in any country.
retatrutide.howSold: Not approved or sold as a finished medicine. Gray-market vendors sell it as a research compound in powder vials (commonly 10 or 30 mg).
retatrutide.bottomLine: Retatrutide is still investigational and not approved anywhere. Any use outside a clinical trial is unproven, and decisions belong with a licensed professional.

tirzepatide.teaser: An FDA-approved dual-receptor medicine for diabetes and weight.
tirzepatide.whatItIs: A dual GLP-1 and GIP receptor agonist.
tirzepatide.studiedFor: FDA-approved for type 2 diabetes (Mounjaro) and weight management (Zepbound), and studied in large clinical trials.
tirzepatide.howSold: By prescription as a pre-filled pen or vial (Mounjaro, Zepbound). It is also sold by gray-market vendors as a research powder, which is not the approved product.
tirzepatide.bottomLine: Tirzepatide is an FDA-approved prescription medicine. The approved product comes through a licensed provider and pharmacy, and decisions about it belong with them.

hgh.teaser: Prescription growth hormone, measured in international units.
hgh.whatItIs: Recombinant human growth hormone (somatropin), a lab-made copy of a hormone the body produces.
hgh.studiedFor: FDA-approved by prescription for specific growth hormone deficiencies and certain other conditions. It is measured in international units (IU).
hgh.howSold: By prescription as a powder or pen for reconstitution. Vial strengths are given in IU.
hgh.bottomLine: HGH is a prescription medication, and non-medical use is restricted by law in many places. Decisions belong with a licensed provider.

hcg.teaser: A prescription hormone dosed in international units.
hcg.whatItIs: Human chorionic gonadotropin, a hormone produced as a medicine. It is dosed in international units (IU).
hcg.studiedFor: Used in fertility treatment and prescribed in some hormone protocols.
hcg.howSold: By prescription as a powder for reconstitution, in IU strengths (commonly 5,000 or 10,000 IU).
hcg.bottomLine: HCG is a prescription medication. Whether it is appropriate for a given person is a decision for them and a licensed healthcare provider.

nad-plus.teaser: A coenzyme found in every living cell, sold as an injectable.
nad-plus.whatItIs: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide, a coenzyme present in every living cell. It is not a peptide, though it is commonly sold and reconstituted alongside them. It takes part in energy metabolism and DNA repair, and levels decline with age.
nad-plus.studiedFor: Studied for metabolic function, cellular energy, and the biology of aging. Most human research has used precursors taken by mouth, such as nicotinamide riboside and NMN, rather than injected NAD+. Evidence for the injectable form is thinner than the attention it receives.
nad-plus.howSold: As a freeze-dried powder in vials, commonly 500 mg or 1000 mg, reconstituted with bacteriostatic water. Also offered as an IV infusion in clinics and through compounding pharmacies. Once reconstituted it keeps for roughly two weeks refrigerated, a shorter window than most peptides.
nad-plus.bottomLine: Not FDA-approved as an injectable drug, and the human evidence for injection specifically is limited. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

ss-31.teaser: A mitochondria-targeting peptide, FDA-approved for one rare disease.
ss-31.whatItIs: A synthetic peptide, also called elamipretide, that concentrates in the inner mitochondrial membrane where it interacts with a lipid called cardiolipin.
ss-31.studiedFor: Studied for mitochondrial dysfunction. In September 2025 the FDA granted accelerated approval to elamipretide, under the brand name Forzinity, for Barth syndrome in patients weighing at least 30 kg. It was the first approved therapy for any mitochondrial disease. Work in other settings, including aging and heart and muscle function, remains investigational.
ss-31.howSold: As Forzinity by prescription for its approved use. Research suppliers also sell it as a powder in vials, commonly 10, 40, or 50 mg, which is not the approved product.
ss-31.bottomLine: Approved for one rare condition in one narrow population. Everything beyond that is off-label and still under study. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.

mots-c.teaser: A peptide written into mitochondrial DNA, studied in metabolism.
mots-c.whatItIs: A short peptide, 16 amino acids long, encoded not by the cell nucleus but by mitochondrial DNA. Peptides of this kind are called mitochondrial-derived peptides.
mots-c.studiedFor: Examined for insulin sensitivity, metabolic regulation, and exercise biology, mostly in animal and laboratory work. The one human study published to date used intravenous administration, while nearly all circulating protocols describe subcutaneous injection. The dosing figures widely quoted online are therefore extrapolated rather than tested.
mots-c.howSold: As a freeze-dried powder in vials, commonly 5 mg or 10 mg, reconstituted with bacteriostatic water. Repeated freezing and thawing degrades it, so reconstituted solution is kept refrigerated rather than refrozen.
mots-c.bottomLine: Not FDA-approved for any use, and the human evidence is very limited. Whether it is appropriate, legal, or safe for any person is a decision for that person and a licensed healthcare provider.
